topicName: Composite Indexes and Leftmost Prefix Rule
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Composite Indexes and the Leftmost Prefix Rule"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing high-performance relational databases, optimizing read operations is crucial. While single-column indexes are useful, complex queries often filter or sort by multiple columns. This is where composite indexes come into play, governed strictly by the Leftmost Prefix Rule."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is a Composite Index?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A composite index (also known as a concatenated or multi-column index) is an index defined on multiple columns of a table. Instead of creating separate indexes for columns A, B, and C, a single composite index is built using the sequence (A, B, C)."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"CREATE INDEX idx_users_loc_age_name ON users (location, age, last_name);"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"The Leftmost Prefix Rule Explained"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Leftmost Prefix Rule dictates that for a composite index to be successfully utilized by the database query optimizer, the query must reference the columns in the exact order they are defined in the index, starting from the leftmost column."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If the index is defined as (A, B, C), the database can use the index for queries filtering on: (A), (A, B), and (A, B, C)."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The database CANNOT efficiently use the index for queries filtering solely on: (B), (C), (B, C), or (C, A)."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Examples of Query Optimization"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider the composite index idx_users_loc_age_name (location, age, last_name). Let us analyze which queries will leverage this index."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM users WHERE location = 'New York'; -- Uses the index (leftmost prefix)"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM users WHERE location = 'New York' AND age = 30; -- Uses the index (matches prefix)"},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM users WHERE age = 30; -- Does NOT use the index effectively (skips location)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Database Design"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Place columns with the highest cardinality (most unique values) first only if they match your primary filtering patterns, but always prioritize access path requirements."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Align your composite index column order with your most frequent and critical WHERE clauses."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid over-indexing, as composite indexes consume additional storage and slow down write (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) operations."}]
